front: What is a proposition?
back: A declarative statement of fact with a truth value — either true or false, never both.

front: What does ¬p mean?
back: It is not the case that p. Negation has the opposite truth value to p.

front: When is p ∧ q true?
back: Both p and q must be true; false otherwise.

front: When is p ∨ q true?
back: At least one is true, including when both are true. Or is inclusive by default.

front: When is p ⊕ q true?
back: Exactly one proposition is true, not both.

front: When is p → q false?
back: Only when p is true and q is false: the condition is met but the result does not follow.

front: When is p ↔ q true?
back: When p and q have the same truth value.

front: Give the converse of p → q.
back: q → p.

front: Give the inverse of p → q.
Give the contrapositive of p → q.
back: ¬q → ¬p. This is equivalent to the original implication.

front: Which Table 7/8 identities may you cite?
back: Only p → q ≡ ¬p ∨ q; p → q ≡ ¬q → ¬p; p ↔ q ≡ (p → q) ∧ (q → p). All of Table 6 is allowed. Other Table 7/8 identities must be derived.

front: State De Morgan for ¬(p ∧ q).
back: ¬(p ∧ q) ≡ ¬p ∨ ¬q — negate each piece and flip the connective.

front: State De Morgan for ¬(p ∨ q).
What is a tautology?
back: A compound proposition that is always true, no matter the truth values of its individual propositions.

front: What does ∀xP(x) mean?
back: For every x in the domain, P(x) is true.

front: What does ∃xP(x) mean?
back: There exists some (at least one) x in the domain so that P(x) is true.

front: Negate ∀xP(x).
back: ∃x¬P(x). Flip the quantifier, negate the inside.

front: Negate ∃xP(x).
Does ∀x distribute over ∨?
back: No. ∀x(P(x) ∨ Q(x)) ≢ ∀xP(x) ∨ ∀xQ(x). Different x may satisfy different predicates.

front: Can mixed quantifiers be swapped?
back: Not in general. ∀x∃y allows y to depend on x; ∃y∀x requires one y for every x.

front: State modus ponens.
back: p → q, p, ∴ q.

front: State modus tollens.
Can a valid argument have false premises?
back: Yes. Validity says that if all premises are true, the conclusion must be true.

front: Define an even integer.
back: An integer n is even if there exists some integer k so that n = 2k.

front: Define an odd integer.
back: An integer n is odd if there exists some integer k so that n = 2k + 1.

front: Define a rational number.
back: A real number x is rational if there exist integers p, q with q ≠ 0 so that x = p/q.

front: Does ℕ include 0 in this class?
What is a set?
back: An unordered collection of distinct objects which we call elements.

front: What is P(S)?
back: The set of all subsets of S. If |S| = n, then |P(S)| = 2ⁿ.

front: Are ∅ and {∅} equal?
back: No. ∅ has 0 elements. {∅} has 1 element: the empty set.

front: State the key facts: Propositions
back: A proposition is a declarative statement of fact with a truth value — either true or false, never both. A false statement is still a proposition.

front: Is a false declarative statement still a proposition?
back: Yes. “8 is prime” is a false proposition.

front: State the key facts: Negation
back: ¬p means “It is not the case that p” and reverses its truth value. Negate an inequality by including equality in the complement when needed.

front: Negate x < 3.
State the key facts: Conjunction
back: p∧q is the proposition of both p and q. Both must be true, false otherwise.

front: Translate “p but not q.”
back: p ∧ ¬q.

front: State the key facts: Disjunction
back: p∨q is true if at least one operand is true. Or is inclusive by default: one or the other or both.

front: What is the only false row of p ∨ q?
back: p=F and q=F.

front: State the key facts: Inclusive and exclusive or
back: p⊕q is exclusive or: exactly one proposition is true, not both. In class, “either … or” is a cue to examine exclusivity; explicit “or both” overrides it.

front: How do ∨ and ⊕ differ on TT?
back: ∨ is true; ⊕ is false.

front: State the key facts: Conditional and English forms
back: p→q is false only if p is true and q is false. p is the condition and q its result. “p only if q,” “q is necessary for p,” “p is sufficient for q,” “q whenever p,” and “q unless ¬p” all express p→q.

front: Translate “q is necessary for p.”
back: p → q.

front: State the key facts: Biconditional
back: p↔q means p if and only if q: (p→q)∧(q→p). It is true exactly when the inputs agree.

front: Expand p ↔ q using conditionals.
State the key facts: Converse
back: The converse of p→q is q→p. It reverses hypothesis and conclusion.

front: Is the converse equivalent to the original?
back: Not generally; p=F,q=T separates them.

front: State the key facts: Inverse
back: The inverse of p→q is ¬p→¬q. It negates both parts without swapping them.

front: Which related statement is equivalent to the inverse?
back: The converse.

front: State the key facts: Contrapositive
back: The contrapositive of p→q is ¬q→¬p. It is the only one of converse, inverse, and contrapositive always equivalent to the original.

front: Contrapose (p ∧ q) → r.
State the key facts: Compound truth tables
back: A truth table lists every assignment to its propositional variables. With n distinct variables it has 2ⁿ rows. Compute inner subexpressions before the outer connective.

front: How many rows for p,q,r?
State the key facts: Operator precedence
back: Parentheses first; then ¬, ∧, ∨, →, ↔ in decreasing binding strength. Use parentheses when mixing XOR or chaining implications to avoid ambiguity.

front: Parse ¬p ∨ q ∧ r.
State the key facts: Tautology, contradiction, contingency
back: A tautology is always true; a contradiction is always false; a contingency is true on some assignments and false on others.

front: Define a contingency.
back: A compound proposition that is true on some assignments and false on others.

front: State the key facts: Logical equivalence
back: p≡q means p↔q is a tautology. Prove this with matching truth-table columns or a chain of already-known equivalences.

front: What suffices to disprove equivalence?
back: One assignment where the formulas have different truth values.

front: State the key facts: The only citable Table 7/8 identities
back: All Table 6 identities are allowed. From Tables 7/8 ONLY: p→q≡¬p∨q (7.1); p→q≡¬q→¬p (contrapositive); p↔q≡(p→q)∧(q→p) (biconditional). Other identities must be derived.

front: May all of Tables 7 and 8 be cited?
back: No. Only conditional-disjunction, contrapositive, and the biconditional definition.

front: State the key facts: Successive substitution
back: Write one equivalent expression per line, give the law that justifies the change, and end with ∎. Each substitution may replace a subexpression by an equivalent one.

front: How do you negate an implication using allowed laws?
State the key facts: Tautologies by equivalences
back: To prove a tautology by equivalences, reduce the expression to T using only allowed laws.

front: What should the final line of a tautology equivalence proof be?
back: ≡ T, with its law and ∎.

front: State the key facts: Identity law (Table 6)
back: p ∧ T ≡ p; p ∨ F ≡ p. The neutral truth value leaves p unchanged.

front: State identity in all Table 6 forms.
back: p ∧ T ≡ p; p ∨ F ≡ p.

front: State the key facts: Domination law (Table 6)
back: p ∨ T ≡ T; p ∧ F ≡ F. A true disjunct or false conjunct determines the result.

front: State domination in all Table 6 forms.
back: p ∨ T ≡ T; p ∧ F ≡ F.

front: State the key facts: Idempotent law (Table 6)
back: p ∨ p ≡ p; p ∧ p ≡ p. Repeating a proposition adds no information.

front: State idempotent in all Table 6 forms.
back: p ∨ p ≡ p; p ∧ p ≡ p.

front: State the key facts: Double negation law (Table 6)
back: ¬¬p ≡ p. Two negations cancel.

front: State double negation in all Table 6 forms.
State the key facts: Commutative law (Table 6)
back: p ∨ q ≡ q ∨ p; p ∧ q ≡ q ∧ p. Swap operands of the same connective.

front: State commutative in all Table 6 forms.
back: p ∨ q ≡ q ∨ p; p ∧ q ≡ q ∧ p.

front: State the key facts: Associative law (Table 6)
back: p ∨ (q ∨ r) ≡ (p ∨ q) ∨ r; p ∧ (q ∧ r) ≡ (p ∧ q) ∧ r. Regroup all ands or all ors.

front: State associative in all Table 6 forms.
State the key facts: Distributive law (Table 6)
back: p ∨ (q ∧ r) ≡ (p ∨ q) ∧ (p ∨ r); p ∧ (q ∨ r) ≡ (p ∧ q) ∨ (p ∧ r). Think of ands with ors; both distributive patterns are valid.

front: State distributive in all Table 6 forms.
State the key facts: De Morgan law (Table 6)
back: ¬(p ∧ q) ≡ ¬p ∨ ¬q; ¬(p ∨ q) ≡ ¬p ∧ ¬q. Negate each piece and flip the connective.

front: State de morgan in all Table 6 forms.
State the key facts: Absorption law (Table 6)
back: p ∨ (p ∧ q) ≡ p; p ∧ (p ∨ q) ≡ p. The standalone p absorbs the more complicated term.

front: State absorption in all Table 6 forms.
back: p ∨ (p ∧ q) ≡ p; p ∧ (p ∨ q) ≡ p.

front: State the key facts: Negation law law (Table 6)
back: p ∨ ¬p ≡ T; p ∧ ¬p ≡ F. A proposition and its negation exhaust the possibilities.

front: State negation law in all Table 6 forms.
back: p ∨ ¬p ≡ T; p ∧ ¬p ≡ F.

front: State the key facts: Predicates and propositional functions
back: The predicate is the property or relationship part of a sentence; the subject is what it is about. A propositional function P(x) depends on an input that can change.

front: What changes a predicate into a proposition?
back: Specify all free inputs, or bind them with quantifiers over a domain.

front: State the key facts: Domains
back: The domain is the allowed set of inputs. Stipulations on the subject are part of the meaning of a quantified statement.

front: Why does ∀x(x²≥x) fail over ℝ?
State the key facts: Universal quantification
back: The universal quantification of P(x) says: for every x in the domain, P(x) is true. Notation ∀x∈D P(x).

front: How many counterexamples refute ∀xP(x)?
back: One element of the domain where P is false.

front: State the key facts: Existential quantification
back: There exists some (at least one) x in the domain so that P(x) is true: ∃xP(x).

front: What establishes ∃xP(x)?
back: One witness x in the domain for which P(x) is true.

front: State the key facts: Counterexamples
back: A counterexample to ∀xP(x) is a domain element a with P(a) false. To refute ∃xP(x), show every candidate fails.

front: Refute ∀x∈ℕ(x²>0).
back: x=0 is a counterexample.

front: State the key facts: Bound and free variables
back: A variable occurrence is bound when it falls in the scope of its matching quantifier; otherwise it is free. A statement with a free variable need not have a fixed truth value.

front: Which variable is free in ∀xP(x,y)?
back: y is free; x is bound.

front: State the key facts: Quantifier distribution: two laws, two failures
back: ∀x(P∧Q) ≡ ∀xP∧∀xQ; ∃x(P∨Q) ≡ ∃xP∨∃xQ. But ∀x(P∨Q) ≢ ∀xP∨∀xQ, and ∃x(P∧Q) ≢ ∃xP∧∃xQ.

front: Which connectives distribute through ∀ and ∃?
back: ∀ through ∧; ∃ through ∨. The other two proposed distributions are not equivalences.

front: State the key facts: Negating quantified statements
back: ¬∀xP(x) ≡ ∃x¬P(x); ¬∃xP(x) ≡ ∀x¬P(x). Flip the quantifier, negate the inside.

front: Negate “Some student is taking Calc 3.”
back: No student is taking Calc 3: ∀x¬T(x), domain students in this class.

front: State the key facts: One-quantifier translations
back: State the domain and define each predicate first. All A are B becomes ∀x(A(x)→B(x)); some A are B becomes ∃x(A(x)∧B(x)).

front: Why use ∧ in “some A are B”?
back: The same witness must actually be A and B.

front: State the key facts: Nested quantifiers
back: A quantifier is nested when it falls in the scope of another. Predicates with multiple inputs allow one quantifier per variable.

front: What does ∀x∃yP(x,y) allow y to depend on?
back: The previously chosen x.

front: State the key facts: Quantifier order
back: Same-kind quantifiers commute: ∀x∀y and ∃x∃y can be swapped. Mixed quantifiers cannot generally be swapped. ∃y∀xP(x,y) implies ∀x∃yP(x,y).

front: Which is stronger: ∃y∀xP or ∀x∃yP?
back: ∃y∀xP; one common witness works for every x.

front: State the key facts: Truth values of the four nests
back: For x+y=0 over ℝ: ∀∀ false, ∀∃ true, ∃∀ false, ∃∃ true. The justification matters as much as the letters.

front: Why is ∃x∀y(x+y=0) false over ℝ?
back: For any proposed x, choose y=1−x; then the sum is 1.

front: State the key facts: Nested translations
back: Specify each variable domain and predicate before translating. Universal choices come before witnesses that may depend on them.

front: Translate nonzero real numbers have multiplicative inverses.
State the key facts: Exactly one: existence and uniqueness
back: Exactly one combines existence with the requirement that every other candidate equals the witness. For P: ∃x(P(x)∧∀z(P(z)→z=x)).

front: What two ingredients does exactly one require?
back: Existence, then uniqueness of the witness.

front: State the key facts: Negating nested statements
back: Push negation inward one quantifier at a time, preserving their order while flipping each. Then negate the predicate or connective.

front: Negate ∀x∃y∀zP(x,y,z).
back: ∃x∀y∃z¬P(x,y,z).

front: State the key facts: Class practice sheet
back: The sheet combines dependent witnesses, changing domains, and uniqueness. Its limit question was crossed out and is omitted.

front: Does “none of a student’s friends are friends with each other” assert that the student has friends?
back: No. It can hold vacuously.

front: State the key facts: Argument, premises, conclusion
back: An argument is a sequence of propositions called premises, followed by a conclusion. An argument form replaces particular statements by propositional variables.

front: What is an argument form?
back: A pattern obtained by replacing statements with propositional variables.

front: State the key facts: Validity is about the form
back: An argument is valid if the truth of all premises implies the truth of the conclusion. Equivalently, (p₁∧…∧pₙ)→q is a tautology. It may have false premises.

front: How can a valid argument have a false conclusion?
back: At least one premise must be false.

front: State the key facts: Step / Reason tables
back: Write each premise or derived statement as a numbered step, with a reason referencing earlier steps. End with ∎.

front: What goes in the Reason column for a given hypothesis?
back: prem. (premise).

front: State the key facts: Equivalences inside arguments
back: Logical equivalences go both ways; rules of inference go one way. An allowed equivalence may replace a statement inside a derivation.

front: May you use contraposition as an argument step?
back: Yes, as an allowed logical equivalence, with a reference to the original step.

front: State the key facts: Showing invalidity
back: An argument form is invalid when some truth assignment makes every premise true and the conclusion false. One such row suffices.

front: Which truth pattern disproves validity?
back: All premises true, conclusion false.

front: State the key facts: Two fallacies
back: Affirming the conclusion: p→q, q, ∴p. Denying the hypothesis: p→q, ¬p, ∴¬q. Both are invalid.

front: Name p→q, ¬p, ∴¬q.
back: Denying the hypothesis; invalid.

front: State the key facts: Proving an inference rule
back: To verify a rule, make the conjunction of its premises imply its conclusion and show the result is a tautology.

front: What proposition tests p→q,p,∴q?
State the key facts: Modus ponens
back: p→q; p ∴ q. This inference preserves truth: whenever all listed premises are true, the conclusion is true.

front: Which rule is p→q; p ∴ q?
back: Modus ponens.

front: State the key facts: Modus tollens
back: p→q; ¬q ∴ ¬p. This inference preserves truth: whenever all listed premises are true, the conclusion is true.

front: Which rule is p→q; ¬q ∴ ¬p?
back: Modus tollens.

front: State the key facts: Hypothetical syllogism
back: p→q; q→r ∴ p→r. This inference preserves truth: whenever all listed premises are true, the conclusion is true.

front: Which rule is p→q; q→r ∴ p→r?
back: Hypothetical syllogism.

front: State the key facts: Disjunctive syllogism
back: p∨q; ¬p ∴ q. This inference preserves truth: whenever all listed premises are true, the conclusion is true.

front: Which rule is p∨q; ¬p ∴ q?
back: Disjunctive syllogism.

front: State the key facts: Addition
back: p ∴ p∨q. This inference preserves truth: whenever all listed premises are true, the conclusion is true.

front: Which rule is p ∴ p∨q?
back: Addition.

front: State the key facts: Simplification
back: p∧q ∴ p. This inference preserves truth: whenever all listed premises are true, the conclusion is true.

front: Which rule is p∧q ∴ p?
back: Simplification.

front: State the key facts: Conjunction
back: p; q ∴ p∧q. This inference preserves truth: whenever all listed premises are true, the conclusion is true.

front: Which rule is p; q ∴ p∧q?
back: Conjunction.

front: State the key facts: Resolution
back: p∨q; ¬p∨r ∴ q∨r. This inference preserves truth: whenever all listed premises are true, the conclusion is true.

front: Which rule is p∨q; ¬p∨r ∴ q∨r?
back: Resolution.

front: State the key facts: Vocabulary of proofs
back: A theorem is a fact that can be proven true (main fact). A proposition is a theorem of lesser prominence (supporting details). An axiom is assumed without proof; a proof establishes truth by valid reasoning.

front: What is a lemma?
back: A theorem used to prove another result.

front: State the key facts: Direct proof
back: To prove p→q directly, suppose p is true and use definitions and algebra to establish q.

front: What is the opening of a direct proof of p→q?
back: Pf Suppose p. Then use definitions and established facts to derive q.

front: State the key facts: Even integers
back: An integer n is even if there exists some integer k so that n=2k.

front: What must the witness k satisfy in n=2k?
back: k∈ℤ.

front: State the key facts: Odd integers and odd squares
back: An integer n is odd if there exists some integer k so that n=2k+1. Every integer is either even or odd.

front: Complete (2k+1)²=2(___)+1.
back: 2k²+2k.

front: State the key facts: Perfect squares
back: An integer n is a perfect square if there exists an integer k so that n=k².

front: Why is the product of two squares a square?
back: k²j²=(kj)² with kj∈ℤ.

front: State the key facts: Rational and irrational
back: A real number x is rational if x=p/q for integers p,q with q≠0. An irrational real is not rational.

front: What denominator restriction defines rationality?
back: The integer denominator is nonzero.

front: State the key facts: Contraposition: 3n+2
back: To prove p→q, first state C.P.: If ¬q then ¬p. Then prove that implication directly.

front: How does a contraposition proof begin?
back: C.P.: If ¬q then ¬p. Pf We will prove the contrapositive. Suppose ¬q.

front: State the key facts: At least one small factor
back: If n=ab with positive integers a,b, then a≤√n or b≤√n. The conclusion is an inclusive or.

front: Negate a≤√n or b≤√n.
back: a>√n and b>√n.

front: State the key facts: Contradiction of a proposition
back: To prove p, assume ¬p and derive a contradiction r∧¬r. Name the contradiction at the end.

front: What do you assume to prove p by contradiction?
State the key facts: Canonical proof: √2 irrational
back: Use a reduced fraction, then show both numerator and denominator are even. The parity lemma follows by contraposing the odd-square proof.

front: What is the contradiction in the √2 proof?
back: The fraction was reduced, but p and q are both even and share factor 2.

front: State the key facts: Contradiction of an implication
back: To prove p→q by contradiction, assume both p and ¬q. This is the negation of the whole implication.

front: Negate p→q before a contradiction proof.
back: p∧¬q.

front: State the key facts: Canonical proof: irrational plus rational
back: The sum of an irrational and a rational is irrational.

front: Must a sum of two irrationals be irrational?
State the key facts: Proving biconditionals
back: To prove p↔q, prove both p→q and q→p, labeled (→) and (←). Different methods may be used for the directions.

front: How many directions must an iff proof establish?
back: Both (→) and (←).

front: State the key facts: TFAE cycle
back: To show several statements are equivalent, prove a cycle p₁→p₂→p₃→p₁. Transitivity then supplies every remaining direction.

front: Which three arrows suffice for a,b,c TFAE?
back: a→b, b→c, c→a.

front: State the key facts: Canonical proof: ∛2 irrational
back: First prove the lemma n³ even ⇒ n even by contraposition; then repeat the reduced-fraction contradiction.

front: What lemma is needed for the ∛2 proof?
back: n³ even ⇒ n even; contrapose and expand (2k+1)³.

front: State the key facts: Sets and elements
back: A set is an unordered collection of distinct objects which we call elements. x∈A means x is an element; x∉A means it is not.

front: Do duplicates change a set?
back: No; its elements are distinct.

front: State the key facts: Roster, set-builder, intervals
back: Roster notation lists elements. Set-builder notation describes exactly which objects qualify. Interval notation describes real numbers between endpoints.

front: Which endpoints are included in (a,b]?
back: b is included; a is excluded.

front: State the key facts: Standard number sets
back: ℕ={0,1,2,…}, ℤ={…,−1,0,1,…}, ℤ⁺={1,2,…}; ℚ rational, ℚ⁺ positive rational, ℝ real, ℝ⁺ positive real, ℂ complex. ℕ includes 0 in this class.

front: Is ℕ=ℤ⁺ in this class?
back: No; 0∈ℕ but 0∉ℤ⁺.

front: State the key facts: Empty set and singleton
back: The empty set ∅={} is the only set with no elements. A singleton has exactly one element.

front: What is a singleton?
back: A set containing exactly one element.

front: State the key facts: Set equality
back: A=B iff every element of A is in B and every element of B is in A; equivalently A⊆B and B⊆A.

front: Does |A|=|B| imply A=B?
back: No: {1} and {2} both have one element but differ.

front: State the key facts: Universal set
back: The universal set U contains all objects currently under consideration. It depends on the problem context.

front: Is U always ℝ?
back: No; it is the set of objects under consideration.

front: State the key facts: Subset, superset, subset proofs
back: A⊆B means ∀x(x∈A→x∈B). B⊇A says the same thing. To prove A⊆B, choose arbitrary x∈A and show x∈B.

front: How do you disprove A⊆B?
back: Find x∈A with x∉B.

front: State the key facts: Proper subsets and supersets
back: A⊂B (also A⊊B) means A⊆B and A≠B. Equivalently every element of A lies in B and some element of B lies outside A. B is a proper superset of A.

front: What extra condition turns ⊆ into ⊂?
back: A≠B; B has an element outside A.

front: State the key facts: ∅⊆A and A⊆A
back: For every set A, ∅⊆A and A⊆A. The first uses a vacuously true implication; the second uses reflexivity.

front: Why is ∅⊆A always true?
back: There are no elements of ∅ that could violate the inclusion.

front: State the key facts: Finite sets and cardinality
back: A finite set has n distinct elements for some nonnegative integer n; its cardinality is |S|=n. A set that is not finite is infinite.

front: What is |{{1}}|?
back: 1. Its only element is {1}.

front: State the key facts: Power sets and 2ⁿ
back: P(S) is the set of all subsets of S. If |S|=n then |P(S)|=2ⁿ: each element has two independent choices, included or omitted.

front: What is P({∅})?
back: {∅,{∅}}, with two elements.

front: State the key facts: Nested sets
back: An inner set is one element when it appears inside outer braces. Membership removes one brace level; subset compares elements without removing a level.
No, since 1 is not an element of {{1}}.

front: Define theorem.
back: A fact that can be proven true; the main fact.

front: Define proposition.
back: A theorem of lesser prominence; supporting details.

front: Define axiom.
back: A statement assumed true without proof.

front: Define proof.
back: A valid argument establishing the truth of a theorem.

front: Define lemma.
back: A theorem used to prove another result.

front: Define corollary.
back: A theorem that follows directly from a theorem just proved.

front: Define conjecture.
back: A statement proposed to be true but not yet proven.

front: Translate: if p, then q
back: p → q

front: Translate: p is sufficient for q
back: p → q

front: Translate: q if p
back: p → q

front: Translate: q when p
back: p → q

front: Translate: a necessary condition for p is q
back: p → q

front: Translate: q unless ¬p
back: p → q

front: Translate: p only if q
back: p → q
